claim: An STDP protocol consisting of pairing a postsynaptic action potential with visually driven presynaptic inputs modifies a neuron's action potential response in a bidirectional way that depends on the relative action potential timing during pairing in vivo.
source_text: Here, we show that in vivo a spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) protocol—consisting of pairing a postsynaptic AP with visually driven presynaptic inputs—modifies a neurons' AP-response in a bidirectional way that depends on the relative AP-timing during pairing.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo whole-cell recordings showing bidirectional changes in neuronal responses depending on spike timing.

claim: Postsynaptic action potentials repeatedly following presynaptic activation can convert subthreshold into suprathreshold responses.
source_text: Whereas postsynaptic APs repeatedly following presynaptic activation can convert subthreshold into suprathreshold responses, APs repeatedly preceding presynaptic activation reduce AP responses to visual stimulation.
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental measurements showing neurons transitioning from non-spiking to spiking responses after positive timing protocols.

claim: Action potentials repeatedly preceding presynaptic activation reduce action potential responses to visual stimulation.
source_text: Whereas postsynaptic APs repeatedly following presynaptic activation can convert subthreshold into suprathreshold responses, APs repeatedly preceding presynaptic activation reduce AP responses to visual stimulation.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing decreased spiking after negative timing protocols.
